doc.title: Jack Palmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 24, 1997

title: Record dates, lost records and royalties
summary: Musicians were paid per record date, rarely kept records, and only leaders collected royalties.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Were you able over the years to keep track of how many records you played on?

No. Hardly anybody does. You know like professional musicians, when I say that I mean like people that played music for a living, you moved around too much to collect records, then you had to move them around, you know what I mean? Unless like some guys had homes in New York or Queens, then they could start a collection, because when they left to go on the road, they had a place. But if you were moving around in hotels, you couldn’t carry that stuff around.
Plus I suppose sometimes you weren’t even sure that the thing was going to end up as a record. You were just recording—

No, no, no. When we were recording, we were recording to make records, oh yeah. It was a recording set and we got paid for a record date. That’s what they called it, a record date. When they recorded us live, like from a hotel where we were broadcasting, they took that
off the air, but somehow they had to get permission to do it or something. There was pretty tight laws.
Do you still get any royalties or any payments for all those years?

No. Because the only one that got royalties was the leader. The sidemen, when I say sidemen, the musicians, we got paid for the date and that was it. The only one that signed a contract with the recording company was the leader, or the manager or whatever. But the leader always collected royalties. And they were very good about mailing his checks to him, you know.
